tiles.alt: EPISODE TEN / Positive Bias

A train compartment. A girl with an enormous cloud of bushy brown hair sits alone, reading a thick book. / No-one had asked for help. That was the problem. / Aside from helping people with their homework, or anything else they needed, she really didn't know how to meet people.

Hermione, thinking. Below her, a daydream: another girl in the doorway, waving hello. / Hermione: Why did she have to take all the responsibility, when there were two people involved? Why didn't adults ever help? / Hermione: She wished some other girl would just walk up to her and say, "Hermione, the teacher told me to be friends with you."

Through the open compartment door: Hermione reading happily, alone. / Hermione Granger was sitting alone on the first day of school, in the last carriage of the train, with the door left open just in case anyone wanted to talk to her. / But let it be quite clear: she was not sad, lonely, gloomy, depressed, or despairing. She was rereading Hogwarts: A History for the third time, and quite enjoying it.

In the corridor, a boy in robes with a scarf wrapped round his face knocks on a compartment door, his trunk scuttling behind him. / Harry: Excuse me, does anyone here know the six quarks, or where I can find a first-year girl named Hermione Granger?
Hermione: …unless she'd somehow misheard?
Hermione: Can I help you with something? / Harry: Not unless you can name the six quarks, or tell me where to find Hermione Granger.
Hermione: Up, down, strange, charm, truth, beauty. And why are you looking for her?

Harry: Ah, so you're a first-year girl named Hermione Granger. On the train to Hogwarts, no less. / Harry: Presumably I'm meant to invite you to join my party, or get a key magical item from you. PC or NPC, that is the question?
She couldn't think of any possible reply to… whatever that was.

He sat down across from her. His trunk scurried in after him, grew to three times its size, and snuggled up next to hers in an oddly disturbing fashion. / Harry: Please, have a seat. And close the door, if you would. Don't worry, I don't bite anyone who doesn't bite me first.
SLAM. / The imputation that this boy thought she was scared of him made her slam the door into the wall with unnecessary force.
Hermione: I didn't say I was Hermione Granger!

Harry: I didn't say you said you were Hermione Granger. I just said you were. If you're asking how I know, it's because I know everything. / Harry: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. My name is Harry James Potter‑Evans‑Verres, or Harry Potter for short. I know that probably doesn't mean anything to you, for a change—

Harry, unmasked, standing with a showman's flourish: messy black hair, round glasses, green eyes, and the lightning-bolt scar. / Bright, laughing green eyes. And an angry red-dark scar in the shape of a lightning bolt.

Hermione: Harry Potter! You're in Modern Magical History and The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts and Great Wizarding Events of the Twentieth Century! / It was the very first time in her whole life that she'd met someone from inside a book. It was rather an odd feeling.
Harry: I'm in books? Wait. Of course I'm in books… What a strange thought.
Hermione: Goodness, didn't you know? I'd have found out everything I could, if it was me.
Harry: Miss Granger, it has been less than seventy-two hours since I discovered my claim to fame. Believe me, I intend to find out everything I can. / Harry: What do the books say about me?

Hermione recites, rapid-fire, eyes rolled up as if reading from memory. / Hermione: You're the only one who's ever survived the Killing Curse, so you're called the Boy-Who-Lived. Born the thirty-first of July, 1980. On the thirty-first of October 1981, He‑Who‑Must‑Not‑Be‑Named (though I don't know why not) attacked your home.

Hermione: The Rise and Fall of the Dark Arts claims you survived because of your mother's love, that your scar contains all of the Dark Lord's magical power, and that the centaurs fear you. But Modern Magical History warns that there are lots of crackpot theories about you.
Harry: Were you told to wait for Harry Potter on the train, or something like that? / Hermione: No. Who told you about me?

Harry: Professor McGonagall. And I believe I see why. Do you have an eidetic memory, Hermione? / Hermione: It's not photographic. I've always wished it was. I had to read my schoolbooks five times to memorise them all.
Harry: Really. I hope you don't mind if I test that. As the saying goes: trust, but verify. / Harry: Magical Drafts and Potions, by Arsenius Jigger.
Hermione's eyes, sparkling with want. / Instantly, Hermione wanted one of those pouches more than she'd ever wanted anything.
Harry: If you were brewing a potion of spider climbing, what would be the next ingredient after the Acromantula silk?

Hermione: Wait until the potion turns exactly the shade of the cloudless dawn sky, eight degrees from the horizon, eight minutes before sunrise. Stir eight times widdershins and once deasil, and then add eight drams of unicorn bogies.
Harry: Well well well well well well. / Harry: I should like to make you a proposition, Miss Granger.
Hermione: A proposition? / Girls weren't supposed to listen to those.
Harry: Can I offer you something to drink?
Hermione politely accepted the fizzy drink. As she started to drink, the boy said: / Harry: I'd like you to help me take over the universe.
Hermione finished her drink and lowered the can. / Hermione: No thank you. I'm not evil.

Harry: I meant it in the sense of the Baconian project: "the effecting of all things possible." Experimental studies of spells. The underlying laws. Bring magic into science, merge the wizarding and Muggle worlds, raise the whole planet's standard of living.

Harry, arms flung wide, and around him the compartment has become stars, a ringed planet, the galaxy. / Harry: Discover the secret of immortality, colonise the Solar System, explore the galaxy. And most importantly, figure out what the heck is really going on here, because all of this is blatantly impossible.
Hermione: And?
Harry: And? That's not enough?
Harry: With your encyclopaedic memory added to my intelligence and rationality, we'll have it finished in no time. Where by "no time" I mean at least thirty-five years.
Hermione: I haven't seen you do anything intelligent. Maybe I'll let you help me with my research.
There was a certain silence in the compartment.
Harry: So you're asking me to demonstrate my intelligence, then. / Harry: I warn you: challenging my ingenuity is a dangerous project. It tends to make your life a lot more surreal.
Hermione: I'm not impressed yet. / Unnoticed, the green drink once again rose to her lips.
Harry: Well, maybe this will impress you. I've found out I don't need the wand. I can make anything I want happen, just by snapping my fingers.
Hermione sprays green pop all over her new robes. The panel bursts. / Onto her brand-new, never-before-worn robes. On the very first day of school. / Hermione: EEK! MY CLOTHES!
Harry: Don't panic! I can fix it for you. Just watch!

The green stain on her robes fades away in three steps. / The green fluid was still there. But even as she watched, it faded, and within a few moments it was as if she'd never spilled anything at all.
The boy was wearing a rather smug sort of smile.
Hermione: Wordless, wandless magic! At HIS age? When he only got his schoolbooks three days ago? / Hermione: ALL THE DARK LORD'S MAGICAL POWER! IN HIS SCAR!
Hermione: I, I, I need to go to the toilet, wait here, all right—
Harry: It was just a trick, Hermione. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to scare you.
Hermione: A trick?
Harry: You asked me to demonstrate my intelligence. So I did something apparently impossible. I can't really do anything by snapping my fingers. At least, I've never actually tested it.
Harry: Nope. No banana.

Harry: I did warn you that challenging my ingenuity makes your life surreal. Remember that, the next time I warn you about something. / Harry: You think you have what it takes to be a scientist in your own right? Then let's see how you investigate a confusing phenomenon.

Step 1: Form a hypothesis. Step 2: Do an experiment. Step 3: Measure the results. Step 4: Make a cardboard poster. / Hermione's mind skipped gears, ground against itself, and spat back the instructions for a school science project:

Hermione: My hypothesis is that the robes come from the shop with a Charm on them to keep them clean. You found that out by spilling something on yourself earlier. / Hermione: And now I do Step Two: an experiment. I'll pour some on your robes, and I predict the stain will disappear.
Hermione pours a little pop on the corner of Harry's robes. It vanishes. / …and it vanished.
Hermione: My answer is that the robes are Charmed to keep themselves clean.
Harry: Not quite.

A stab of disappointment. He wasn't a teacher. But it was still a test, and getting a question wrong always felt like a little punch in the stomach. / (It said almost everything you needed to know about Hermione Granger that she had never once let that stop her.)

Harry: This is a game based on a famous experiment. I have a rule that fits some triplets of numbers, but not others. I've written it down and folded it up, so you know it's fixed. / Harry: 2-4-6 fits the rule. You give me triplets, and I'll say "Yes" or "No". I am Nature, the rule is one of my laws, and you are investigating me.
Hermione's guesses: 4-6-8, 10-12-14, 1-3-5, -3/-1/+1. All YES.
Hermione: The rule is that the numbers have to go up by two each time.
Harry: Now suppose I tell you this test is harder than it looks, and only twenty percent of grown-ups get it right.
Hermione: The numbers have to go up by the same amount each time! It doesn't have to be two!
Harry: Very well. Take the paper out and see how you did.
The note reads: "Three real numbers in increasing order, lowest to highest." / Hermione's jaw dropped.

Hermione: She had the distinct feeling that something terribly unfair had been done to her, that the boy was a dirty rotten cheating liar. But when she cast her mind back, she couldn't think of a single wrong answer he'd given.

Harry: What you've just discovered is called positive bias. You had a rule in your mind, and you kept thinking of triplets that should make it say "Yes". You never tested any that should make it say "No".
Harry: You have to learn to look on the negative side of things. Stare into the darkness. / Harry: Now. Do you want another shot at the original problem?

She had an odd feeling that this was the hardest she'd ever been asked to think on a test. Or maybe the first time she'd ever been asked to think on a test. / Hermione: So… on my hypothesis… when should the pop not vanish?
Hermione: I want to pour some pop on the floor, and see if it doesn't vanish.
The puddle on the floor fades away too. / …it vanished.
Hermione, delighted, points straight at Harry: her hand jabs out past the frame. / Hermione: Of course! You gave me that can! It's not the robe that's enchanted. It was the pop all along!
The boy stood up and bowed to her, solemnly. He was grinning widely now. / Harry: Then… may I help you with your research, Hermione Granger?
Hermione: I, ah…
The compartment door, shut. A small, round shadow waits behind the frosted glass. A timid knock. / A weak, tentative, faint, rather reluctant knocking. / tap… tap…
A small, round, frightened boy at the door. / Neville looked exactly like he knocked. / Neville: I'm Neville Longbottom. I'm looking for my pet toad… have you seen my toad?
Hermione: Then we'll just have to check all the other carriages! I'll help you. My name is Hermione Granger, by the way.

Harry: Hold on. I'm not sure that's the best way. It'll take ages to check the whole train by hand, and you might miss it anyway. / Harry: It makes more sense to go to the front carriage and ask a prefect. They might have spells that make it much easier to find a toad.
Neville: I remember that voice! You're one of the Lords of Chaos! You're the one who gave me chocolate!
Hermione: What? What what WHAT?
Harry: I never! Do I look like the sort of villain who would give sweets to a child?
Neville: You're Harry Potter? The Harry Potter? You?
Harry: No, just a Harry Potter. There are three of me on this train—
Neville shrieks and bolts, running right out of the panel. / Neville gave a small shriek and ran. / eeeek!
Hermione: Can you please explain to me what's going on? / She wondered if hanging around Harry Potter meant always being this confused.

Harry: Oh, we saw him on the platform, looking terrified. The fear is often worse than the thing itself, so we let him see his worst nightmare come true. And it wasn't so bad. We gave him sweets. That's desensitisation therapy.
Hermione: That's awful! You're awful! That poor boy! What you did was mean!

Harry: I think the word you're looking for is enjoyable. And you're asking the wrong question. The question is: did it do more good than harm? It's called consequentialism. Whether an act is right isn't about whether it looks bad.
Hermione opened her mouth to say something utterly searing. Unfortunately, she seemed to have skipped the part where she thought of it first. / Hermione: What if he has nightmares?
Harry: Then they'll be nightmares about horrible monsters who give you chocolate. Which was sort of the whole point.
Hermione: Is your life always this peculiar?
Harry: I make it that peculiar. You're looking at the product of a lot of hard work and elbow grease.

The quiz and counter-quiz went on for several minutes. / Harry: I can do calculus, and I know Bayesian probability theory, and decision theory, and I've read The Feynman Lectures… / Hermione: …and I can name the twelve uses of dragon's blood…
Another timid knock. Neville was crying now. / Neville: I found a p-prefect, but he t-told me prefects weren't to be bothered over little things like m-missing toads.
Harry's face changes. His voice goes cold. / Harry: What were his colours? Green and silver?
Neville: N-no… his badge was r-red and gold.
Hermione: Red and gold! But those are Gryffindor's colours!

Harry hisses, a frightening sound that could have come from a live snake. Hermione and Neville both flinch. / Harry: I suppose finding some first-year's toad isn't heroic enough to be worthy of a Gryffindor prefect.
Harry: Come on, Neville. I'll come with you this time. We'll see if the Boy‑Who‑Lived gets more attention. / Harry: And if we have to, we'll take apart the whole train screw by screw.
Harry: Stay! / (He said it to his trunk.)

Hermione alone again, staring out of the window at the fields going gold with evening. / She probably should have gone with them. But for a moment Harry Potter had turned so scary that she was actually rather glad she hadn't thought of it. / She felt as if she'd just been run over by a steamroller and turned into a pancake.

From outside the moving train: Hermione's sad face behind the compartment window, the sunset sliding across the glass. / Well. She did at least know why she was feeling a little sad inside. / Hermione: Maybe Gryffindor wasn't as wonderful as she had thought.
To be continued
